Niger
Niger's military on Saturday said it was "gradually regaining control" after mutineers started holding soldiers hostage at a military base next to the capital's airport and fired shots.
In a statement read out on public television and signed by Defence Minister General Salifou Mody, the authorities called on the public to "remain calm and freely go about their business".
Heavy gunfire was heard in seve"Insurgents from within the armed forces" tried to enter the presidential palace in Niger's capital Niamey on Saturday, security sources told AFP, but were repelled by the presidential guard. Shooting is reportedly ongoing at the palace.
Overnight, residents reported hearing heavy gunfire in several neighbourhoods of the capital, near the presidential palace and around the airport, which is home to a major military base.
State television was off air for over an hour before being restored at about 10am local time.

corpus.title: Gunfire erupts in Niger capital, state TV goes off air
corpus.signal_text:
© Turkuvaz Haberleşme ve Yayıncılık 2026
                        
                    
													
								Edited By Kelvin Ndunga
							
						                    
                
            				
									by Agence France-Presse - AFP
								
            			Aug 29, 2026 1:09 pm
        
        Niger’s state television station was off the air Saturday after heavy gunfire and explosions were reported overnight around a military base near the capital’s airport, with soldiers also blocking access to the presidential palace, according to residents and security sources.
The cause of the clashes was not immediately clear. Niger’s military urged the public to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information, saying defense and security forces had been mobilized.
“Given the current events, let us remain calm and avoid sharing unverified information,” the military said on its official social media accounts.
A local resident told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that heavy gunfire and explosions could be heard around Air Force Base 101, located inside the international airport complex. Several other residents reported hearing sustained bursts of gunfire overnight and into Saturday morning.
The first shots were heard around 1:00 a.m. local time and continued until daybreak, according to a video posted online by a local journalist showing the area around the airport. Another resident said he heard bursts of gunfire around 7:00 a.m.
“The weapons we're hearing are not the kind that terrorists on motorbikes can carry,” the resident said. “The fighting has been non-stop since last night.”
Another resident in western Niamey reported sporadic small-arms fire around 5 a.m.
By 9 a.m., Tele Sahel, the national television broadcaster, was showing a black screen on both satellite and online platforms. Residents said soldiers had blocked roads leading to the presidential palace and the television station.
Videos circulating on social media appeared to show armored vehicles moving into areas near the airport, although the footage could not immediately be independently verified.
The developments came as Niger marks three years under military rule following a July 2023 coup led by Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani. The junta has struggled to contain jihadist violence that has plagued the country and the wider Sahel region for more than a decade.
Air Force Base 101 has become a particularly sensitive military site after being targeted twice this year by rival jihadist groups.

corpus.title: Niger's defense ministry says soldiers attempted mutiny
corpus.signal_text:
Niger's defense ministry says soldiers attempted mutiny
August 29, 2026
Gunfire and explosions were heard across Niamey overnight. The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup.
Niger's Ministry of National Defense on Saturday said that a group of soldiers shot at "sensitive" locations in the capital Niamey in an apparent mutiny.
Gunfire and explosions had been heard across Niger's capital, Niamey, overnight into the early hours of Saturday morning.
Attackers had targeted Diori Hamani International Airport, which also houses a military air base, and attempted to breach the security perimeter around the presidency.
"Another cowardly attack on Base 101 and once again our defense and security forces ensured ... Situation under control," said lawmaker Bana Wagana Ibrahim, who serves on the Consultative Council.
Niger military 'gradually regaining control'
The military said it was "gradually regaining control" after mutineers took soldiers hostage at a base near the airport in Niamey, AFP news agency reported.
Authorities urged the public to "remain calm and freely go about their business" in a statement read out on public television and signed by Defense Minister General Salifou Mody.
The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup.
Niger, like its Sahelian neighbors Mali and Burkina Faso, has for years been ruled by a military junta that has struggled to stem a jihadi insurgency.
National TV signal reportedly cut after gunfire
The shooting began around 1 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) and continued until daybreak.
Locals said that the country's national television had gone off air.
Tele Sahel's satellite and online programming was replaced with a black screen at 9 a.m. local time (0800 GMT), AFP reported. It was restored around one hour later.
Niamey has been targeted by jihadists twice this year: once by the so-called "Islamic State in the Sahel" group (EIS) and again in June by their rivals from the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM).
Edited by: Sean Sinico, Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery

corpus.title: Niger: Gunfire and explosions heard in Niamey
corpus.signal_text:
“There is heavy gunfire and there are explosions around Niamey’s Base 101,” one local resident told AFP, an account confirmed by several other witnesses. At around 5am local time (4am GMT), a resident of Koira Kano, another neighbourhood in the west of the Niger capital, said he had heard sporadic small-arms fire.
Several posts on social media also reported gunfire and explosions in the city, including in the administrative district that houses the presidential palace and the national television broadcaster, which was still on air at 5am local time. Other posts showed armoured vehicles being deployed as reinforcements in a neighbourhood close to the airport.
Source of gunfire remains unknown
It is not yet clear what caused the gunfire, and the authorities have issued no official statement. Activists and communicators close to the junta have nevertheless said the “situation is under control”.
Niamey airport has twice been targeted by jihadists this year – first by Islamic State in January, then in late June by its rivals in JNIM, al-Qaeda’s Sahel affiliate. The army repelled both attacks, although 11 soldiers and two civilians were killed in June.
In January, General Abdourahamane Tiani, head of the military regime that took power in a July 2023 coup, acknowledged “a breach in the security system” that had “allowed the attack to take place”. He said its “objective was to destroy all of the army’s air capabilities”.
Air Force Base 101, which lies within the international airport complex, houses the headquarters of Niamey’s Russian partners in the Africa Corps. It is also home to the command of the unified force of the Alliance of Sahel States, which brings together Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali.
The site is particularly sensitive. Between December and January, it was being used to store a large shipment of uranium concentrate that was being held there pending export. No movement of the shipment has been detected since.
With AFP
